en: No other was so unruly.
He must have struck their horse-herder,
Beaten and battered their shepherd,
Left him mottled with blood.
'An orphan acting thus will do us no good;
Grown up, he will not leave us unharmed.
He will plunder our riches.
If we leave this orphan alone,
He will bring disorder upon us all,
Put an end to us together.
When he reaches twelve years of age,
He will slaughter every one of us,
Thus he will put an end to us.
If he grows up, he will do us no good;
He will leave none of us unharmed.'
Abyke, Köbösh, the six villains,
Thus openly took counsel;
Upon the six-year-old champion
They must have acted outrageously.
Beating the boy excessively,
They must have left him mottled with blood.
Making him ford the Talas River,
Battering him as though he were a grown man,
They must have tormented and beaten him.
Without a cap, bareheaded,
Without a shirt, naked,
He must have escaped and fled in haste,
Fled toward his mother Burulcha.
The cowherds' children,
He must have gathered them all.
This very year Külchoro
Must have begun playing knucklebones,
Must have won all the knucklebones.
'My uncle who went to Bukhara—
When will he come?' he asks,
He must be pestering Burulcha.
When you come, he will be overcome with grief;
Crying 'Khan Uncle!' he will run out to meet you.
When you see Külchoro's state,
Your rib bones will seem to come apart;
My orphan, tears will pour from your eyes.
Külchoro running toward you
Will seem like your whole world.
If you accept my words,
That Külchoro,
If he becomes your companion,
Will be a lion blessed with victory,
A hero greater than you.
The tulpar he rides will be gray;
He will be your true companion.
Though a storm comes, no wind will touch you;
He will give no livestock to a shouting enemy.
He will gird his waist in full readiness.
If an army of seventy thousand swarms forth,
With his coat thrown loosely on, he will enter and attack.
He is the support on whom to rely.
Your father's sworn brother Almambet
Dedicated and gave him specially;
He is the lion left as a gift.
Beyond you yourself, my little foal,
By a spear's length, a fathom,
He is the lion who will reach farther.
Until your precious life ends,
Until you see the face of the other world,
Serving you faithfully,
He is the lion who will be your companion.
He will be a blazing red ember;
When he faces them, countless troops will halt.
He will be a lion among spearmen,
A lion of surpassing resourcefulness.
If you ask about Külchoro,
He is your excellence left by a noble one,
Your champion left by a champion,
His honor born of purity,
The only child of a saint.
Your incomparable plane tree,
From your noble father's sworn brother,
Your courser left as a gift.
Dress him in a costly coat;
When you turn back this way,
My little foal, mount him on Kylzheerde
And bring Külchoro here.
Even ridden six months, he would not tire—
I will make him a fleet steed.
Giving him milk from my white breast,
Until the age of the Last Judgment,
I will make him your brother.
If you bring Külchoro,
He is your support when you pull upward,
Your prop when you pull downward,
Your auspicious road if you put him in front,
Your countless army when you enter battle.
Külchoro is your champion,
Among round-headed mortals,
The indispensable one whose like cannot be found.
Do not bring on excessive suffering;
I have given you this charge most firmly:
Do not abandon Külchoro.
Such is Külchoro's story.
Let me leave that here;
Let me begin from this side.
Wearing a coat of blue rep cloth,
Riding a horse like Kökala,
He was your father's sworn brother,
Akbaltai's Chubak.
Your father entered Beijing and returned;
The one he had relied upon,
Khan Chubak, he lost.
Chubak, born of the unseen world,
His lot improved from then—
Who knows whether he is dead or alive?
What became of his condition,
The one Creator alone knows.
In battle against Kakan Khan,
In the havoc and turmoil of war,
If we continue the old account,
From the wise men who went on the campaign,
If we ask those who know,
The great mass of Manchus and Torguts,
When he hemmed them in and drove them back,
Akbaltai's Chubak,
I hear, was struck by a bullet.
Is it false or true? Who knows?
Its clear and spotless truth,
Almighty Allah alone knows;
Who besides Him knows?
Struck by a bullet in battle,
In that fighting at Beijing,
Helpless, with blood flowing,
He entered a grave, I have heard.
Akbaltai's Chubak,
Struck by a bullet in the flank,
Became a coward, I have heard.
The steel bullets to fire on campaign,
He left scattered, I have heard.
Turning toward his homeland,
The distinguished champion Chubak,
The offspring of the mighty unseen,
Fled away, I have heard.
His blood exhausted, utterly worn out,
The distinguished panther Chubak,
Entered Kashgar, I have heard.
To grievously ill Chubak,
With moon dark and day overcast,
A decree was issued, I have heard.
Malabek, khan of Kashgar,
Smearing poison upon Chubak,
Did him harm, I have heard.
Chubak, son of Khan Baltai,
I have a migration coming from Altay,
In his childhood, that Chubak,
That hardened Kashgar,
Ravaged and took it six times, they say;
The Sarts have a grievance against him for this.
I hear scattered scraps of news:
Wounded and senseless,
My precious, devastating Chubak,
Without pausing to gather his senses,
Entered Andijan, I hear.
There was a grievance to avenge;
Andijan's fork-bearded Synchybek
Killed Chubak, I hear.
I hear uncertain scraps of news:
Struck by a bullet, his strength gone,
Blood flowing from his chest,
Leaning upon his lacquered spear,
His strength gone after losing blood,
Chubak, fleeing in haste,
Entered Kokand, I hear.
Kozubek in Kokand,
The proud, fierce Chubak,
Put him to death, I hear.
The reason he killed him—
Beyond the far edge of Kashgar,
On the slopes of broad Alai,
Chubak had a migrating caravan.
Of Khan Kozubek in Kokand, Ayymkan—
She was Chubak's wife.
'He seized her openly,' they say;
Those Sarts have a grievance.
'He killed him,'
I, your poor mother, suspect.
I, your bereaved, unhappy mother,
Have uncertainty in what I say.
Your father's sworn brother Chubak had a son.
Kambar must have taken his mother;
He must have slaughtered a ram for his feast,
Named him the champion Kanchoro.
If you bring him, my champion,
There is a dark-hearted streak in him;
He too will be just the companion for you,
The hero who will stand beside you.
He too is a support to bind about your waist;
If not for his treachery,
He is a hero who spares nothing.
Kambar must have raised him;
My courteous son, listen:
He must have taken him as his father.
Go and see Kanchoro;
Give him a generous gift.
Such is Chubak's story.
Saddle your horse properly and go;
For your fierce father's sworn brother,
Go and recite the Quran unstintingly.
If you make Bakai your guide,
He will show you delightful places.
Tamarisk-covered Keng-Kol, broad Talas—
As you go up through them,
Do not turn aside from the road;
Do not part from your tiger uncle, Khan Bakai!
The reason you must not part—
One who grows wild with his own valor,
Who rides a dark brown horse,
Who knots its hairy tail tight,
Who carries an iron-rope net,
Who carries a spear of blue iron,
Who takes the form of a night demon,
With eyes like twilight mist,
A golden-cheeked battle-axe
Was snugly slung upon her wrist;
A keen sword, never sated with blood,
Was worn unsheathed and bare.
She bound her waist up tightly,
Born to surpass other women,
Her courage equal to a mountain,
Ready to devour a soul in an attack,
The ablest among spear-bearers,
The finest among women,
Of surpassing measure, of the same slope,
Of the same nest as your father Manas.
They had lain within one womb;
With your father, the lion Manas,
She had suckled at one breast.
She dressed in a man's clothing.
If you part from Bakai Khan,
If you come before her eyes,
She is no one to spare you.
She does not know you at all;
She is no soul to hold back.
Whoever stirs her wrath,
She seizes and slaughters.
Your father's own blood sister,
His younger sister Kardygach,
Her dear hair thick as a girth,
Is wearing it tied up now.
Not knowing that Manas has died,
There along the Talas
She is burning with grief now.
Let me tell of Kardygach:
My mother is ninety-five,
The venerable white matron Chyiyrdy,
My mother who cradled them,
Who bore one son, a lion,
Who bore one daughter, a hero—
My mother with the golden womb.
The son she bore, your father,
